provenance.derivation: Editorial. Each family already had an English authoring slug; the Japanese form is a choice, not a translation of that slug. Where an ordinary Japanese colour word exists it is used (茶, 赤, 緑); where the family names a MATERIAL or a QUALITY rather than a hue, the Japanese follows the material (陶土色, 石色) rather than transliterating the English. Katakana is used only where the loanword is genuinely the word a Japanese speaker would reach for. GROUPS (F-224, 2026-09-24): the nine colour-family chips of ADR-0108, each holding the families groupRule places under it. Where a family's own Japanese name decides — a hue word, the head of a hue compound, the hue that tints a grey — the chip follows the name, so the word a family is called by and the chip it sits under cannot disagree. Where the name does not decide, the rule says what does instead and names the family: ADR-0108 fixed off-white (生成り) under 白 and stone (石色) with the greys, and four families go by established usage. No placement comes from a measurement, which is the rule's limit as well as its property: see the 紫 group.
provenance.editorialNotes: The families are the most VISIBLE editorial choice in the product — they are on the Atlas filter, every list row and the detail screen — and until F-090 a Japanese reader saw the English authoring slug on all three. THE JAPANESE HERE IS WRITTEN BY ONE EDITOR AND NOT REVIEWED by a competent speaker; that is the same standing gap the corpus and the phrase lexicon carry (ADR-0060, OQ-5), and it matters more here than in a rationale because a family name is read by everyone who opens the Atlas. A reviewer should expect to change several of these. The groups inherit the same gap: the chip words (Ao 青 … Nezumi 鼠) and the placement of four families by usage rather than by a hue word in their names (陶土色, 錆色, 桃, 岩緑青) are one editor's judgement, stated per group so a reviewer can argue with each.

families.rationale: The ordinary compound for the blue-to-green region, and the one a Japanese reader would use unprompted.
青鼠 rather than 青灰: 鼠 is the traditional word for a grey in Japanese colour naming, and this corpus is built on that vocabulary.
The plain word. 茶 covers the whole brown region in ordinary Japanese use and needs no qualifier here.
墨 is ink-black in the traditional palette and is what these near-blacks are named after; 木炭 would name the material rather than the colour.
A material family, so the Japanese follows the material: 陶土 is potter's clay, which is what these warm mid-tones are drawn from.
Grey qualified by temperature. 鼠 keeps it inside the traditional grey vocabulary, and 寒色系 is the standard way to say the cool side.
Depth rather than a named dye: these are dark blues of several origins, so 紺 or 藍 would claim a specific dye they do not all share.
金茶 rather than 金: the family is a warm yellow-brown, not a metallic, and 金 alone would suggest metal.
The plain word, for the same reason as 茶: the family is the whole green region with no qualifier.
The same construction as 青鼠, keeping 鼠 as the grey element across every grey family.
Lightness qualified, not a dye name. Naming it 縹 or 花色 would assert a traditional dye these entries were not derived from.
岩緑青 is the mineral pigment green of Japanese painting, which is exactly what this family is named for in English.
The mineral half made explicit while keeping 鼠 as the grey element; 鉱物 would read as a geology term rather than a colour.
黄土 is the established Japanese word for ochre as a pigment, and needs no loanword.
生成り is undyed, unbleached cloth — the exact sense of off-white in a clothing context, and far better than オフホワイト for a product about what you wear.
淡い is the standard qualifier for a weak, light colour, and matches the phrase lexicon's use of the same word.
The same construction as 淡い青, so the pale families read as one set.
The same construction again; consistency across the three pale families matters more than finding a distinct word for each.
桃 is the traditional pink and is at home beside the rest of this vocabulary; ピンク would be the only katakana loanword in the set.
The plain word, like 茶 and 緑: the family is the whole red region.
錆 is rust as the material, and 錆色 is the established colour word built on it — the same move as 陶土色.
A material family named after stone, so the Japanese names the material and adds 色, consistent with 錆色 and 陶土色.
The same 鼠 construction as the other grey families, with 紫 for the violet cast.
The counterpart to 寒色系の鼠, so the two temperature-qualified greys read as a pair.
The ordinary compound, and the direct counterpart to 青緑 at the other end of the green region.

groupRule: A family goes under exactly one chip. (1) ADR-0108 fixes the achromatic families: 生成り (off-white) under 白, and the greys whose names carry no hue — 寒色系の鼠, 暖色系の鼠, 石の鼠, and 石色, which names a material, not a class — under 鼠; 墨 (ink-black) names no hue and goes under 黒. (2) Otherwise the hue in the family's own Japanese name decides: the last hue word of a hue compound (青緑 and 黄緑 to 緑, 金茶 to 茶), the hue that tints a grey (青鼠 to 青, 緑鼠 to 緑, 紫鼠 to 紫), or the hue word the name carries (深い青, 中間の青, 淡い青 to 青; 淡い緑 to 緑; 淡い黄 and 黄土 to 黄). (3) Established usage overrides (1) and (2) where a name is a pigment or a material rather than a hue compound, and each is named: 岩緑青 is verdigris, a green pigment, so it goes to 緑 although 緑青 read as a compound would end in 青; 陶土色 and 錆色 carry no hue word and go to 茶; 桃 goes to 赤. A tinted grey goes to its hue and not to 鼠 because the corpus's only purples are its violet-greys and 紫 is a chip mockup 05 draws — a choice with a cost stated in the 紫 group.

groups.rationale: The blues by the hue word in their names — 深い青, 中間の青, 淡い青 — and 青鼠, a grey tinted blue, by the hue that tints it (rule 2). 青緑 is not here: its head is 緑.

赤 by its name. 桃 carries no hue word and goes by established usage (rule 3): in Japanese colour naming a peach-blossom pink is a light red, and the corpus has no other home for it that names a hue. Its two entries are pale (L 0.90–0.91, C 0.02–0.03), and 花冷 leans lilac.

緑 and 淡い緑 by their hue word; 黄緑 and 青緑 by the last hue word of the compound, which is 緑 in both; 緑鼠 by the hue that tints it (rule 2); and 岩緑青 by usage (rule 3) — 緑青 is verdigris, the green pigment, so the rule names it rather than reading its last character, which is 青.

紫鼠, a grey tinted purple, by the hue that tints it (rule 2). It is the corpus's only purple family, which is why rule 2 sends tinted greys to their hue: a 紫 chip holding nothing would be a control that filters to an empty page. THE COST, stated: the family is placed by its NAME, and its three entries measure OKLCh hue 258°–282°. 冬影 (282°) reads violet; 寒星 (272°) sits where 星無 sits under 青; 霜夜 (258°) is bluer than half the deep blues. A person tapping 紫 will see navy-violets rather than purples until the family is re-examined (F-299).

茶 by its name and 金茶 by the head of its compound. 陶土色 (potter's clay) and 錆色 (rust) carry no hue word and go by usage (rule 3): both are the warm earths Japanese colour naming counts among its browns, the family of the Edo phrase shijūhatcha, forty-eight browns.

墨 is ink-black and names no hue (rule 1). The charcoal family runs from near-black (底墨, L 0.19) to a dark iron grey (鉄砂, L 0.44); it is the family the corpus names for its darkest neutrals, and 黒 is the chip that means them on this row.
淡い黄 by its hue word, and 黄土 — yellow earth — by the hue word it carries (rule 2), not by 土, which names a material. Past the drawn edge of 05, as conflict C13 already placed it (ADR-0108).

生成り, unbleached cloth, names no hue (rule 1) and is what the corpus holds of white. Past the drawn edge (ADR-0108): 05 draws no white, and a white under any drawn chip would be labelled black or a hue it does not have.

The greys named for temperature or material rather than a hue — 石色, 暖色系の鼠, 寒色系の鼠, 石の鼠 (rule 1, as ADR-0108 fixed them). 鼠 is the corpus's own word for grey (see blue-grey above) and the period's: shijūhatcha hyakunezumi, a hundred greys. Past the drawn edge (ADR-0108). Placed by name, so it holds 岩肌 (L 0.21, a green-black mineral grey) beside 朝靄 (L 0.89).
